newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia 10-yr bond yield now eyeing 7.0 pct.
newsitem.headline: Australia 10-yr bond yield now eyeing 7.0 pct.

text.p: *Long-dated Australian bonds rallied during the afternoon as post-rate cut profit-taking was absorbed and as U.S. bonds took off in Tokyo after the U.S. election came out as expected.
*October labour force report due on Thursday.
Long-dated Australian bonds rallied as post-rate cut profit-taking was absorbed and as U.S. bonds took off in Tokyo after the U.S. election came out as expected.
The benchmark November 2006 bond yield closed at its lowest level since early March 1994 at just below 7.20 percent and analysts believe it could be testing 7.0 percent before long.
"Aussie bonds have done very well in the last six months and have rallied around 175 basis points both in yield and spread," said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia.

"Our view would be that there's probably a bit more to go," Koukoulas added, citing a yield below 7.0 percent and a yield spread to the U.S. of 50 to 75 basis points. The Australian/U.S. 10-year bond yield spread closed was around 95 basis points.
As widely expected, the Reserve Bank shaved 50 basis points off official interest rates to 6.50 percent, is second policy easing of the year.

Although some of the market had been looking for a bigger cut, there's was little to suggest that the easing cycle is over in the RBA's accompanying statement and March bill futures are pricing at least a 25 basis points easing by maturity.

The RBA said it reflected the improved inflation outlook and that wages growth at 3.5 percent was compatible with its 2.0-3.0 percent inflation target, although it is still concerned about the size of executive wage increases negotiated through enterprise agreements.

"A further cut in cash rates can't be ruled out at this stage, particularly if economic data remains soft and if the pace of enterprise agreements moderates," said Shane Oliver, chief economist at AMP Investments.
However, he felt that rates would stabilise around these levels for some time.
"The Reserve Bank will want to avoid easing too far, particularly in an environment where enterprise agreements are strong," Oliver added.
The Australian labour force report for October is due on Thursday, data that may prove useful for gauging the chance of another easing down the track.

A small bounce back is expected in employment, although median forecasts centre on the unemployment rate sticking at 8.7 percent, according to a Reuters survey of economists. Employment is expected to rise 12,000 after the 34,100 drop in September.

Bond yield spreads remained slightly wider against the U.S. but were below their initial highs. The local yield curve flattened sharply as the short end came under pressure from profit-taking with the rate cut having already been fully factored prior today's announcement.
